description: Solo team. I build full stack web tools and I have a background in electronics and Arduino. For this challenge I built Zero Hour Protocol, a health monitor for astronauts on long missions. It tracks vital signs, radiation and cabin air for every crew member, uses real NASA data from OSDR and DONKI, and tells the crew in plain words what is wrong and what to do when Earth is too far away to answer fast. It also works offline and has a voice medic.
summary: Zero Hour Protocol is a health monitor for astronauts on long missions, built for the moment when a crew has to look after itself because a message to Earth can take more than 20 minutes each way. It watches vital signs, radiation and cabin air for every crew member and compares each reading with that person's own normal and with what they are doing right now. Its key idea is the zero hour forecast: from the trend of each vital sign it predicts how many minutes are left before it turns critical, and compares that with the time an answer from Earth would take, so the crew knows whether to ask Earth or act on board now. Every finding comes in plain words with a checklist, and astronauts can say how they feel in any language. I tested the triage on real Inspiration4 blood tests from NASA OSDR, and the app pulls live solar flare data from NASA DONKI. The same tool could serve polar stations, ships and remote clinics on Earth.
details:
The problem

On the ISS a flight surgeon can answer in seconds. On the way to Mars the crew is on its own for long stretches, because a message to Earth can take more than 20 minutes each way, and not everyone on board is a doctor. The challenge asks for software that lets astronauts evaluate their own health and act on it, so that is what I built.

What it does

A live monitor for four crew members shows ECG, pleth and breathing waveforms, heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure, heart rate variability, a stress index and the radiation dose rate.

The AI triage scores every reading with the NEWS2 early warning bands, but only after correcting for activity, so a heart rate of 120 during exercise does not raise an alarm. It also detects an irregular heart rhythm and flags readings that are unusual for that one person compared with their own history. Every finding comes with the reason and a checklist, and says who should act: the crew alone, the crew plus the flight surgeon in the next report, or act now and call.

Zero hour forecast. This is where the name comes from. For every vital sign and for the cabin air, the app fits a trend to the last 2 or 5 minutes and estimates how many minutes are left before it reaches the red band of the early warning score. A countdown appears on the crew card, the monitor, the triage panel and as a dashed line on the trend chart. The time left is compared with the round trip to Earth. If an answer would come too late, the app says so and the checklist comes first. If there is time, it tells the crew to send a report now. It only shows a forecast when the trend is strong, steady and away from that person's normal. In my tests it gave no false forecasts in 20 hours of simulated daily life with workouts, sleep and spacewalks, and in the drills the forecast was within about a minute of the real crossing.

Correlated anomaly detection. Real problems rarely show up in one signal. When several crew members change the same way at the same time, the system points to the shared cause, for example the cabin air, instead of blaming one body. For each person it also shows which signals moved together and what pattern that matches, like low oxygen, heat stress or CO2 buildup.

Self assessment. A daily check in for mood, sleep, blood sugar and symptoms, and a voice medic where the astronaut just speaks, even in Arabic, and gets a spoken answer. Gemini only turns speech into a list of symptoms. The decision always comes from my own rules and is checked against the sensors.

Body check. A clickable body map where each part shows what it does, how space affects it, how it is measured on board and what to do.

First aid. Step by step guides for bleeding, fractures, something in the eye, CPR, choking, burns and nosebleeds, with official St John Ambulance and British Red Cross training videos and notes on what changes in weightlessness, for example how CPR is done without gravity.

Long term risks. Bone loss, lifetime radiation dose, sleep and mood since launch, projected to the end of the mission. A daily routine with reminders, points and streaks keeps the crew doing the small things that prevent big problems.

Five hazards. A strip that follows NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity and the closed environment.

Mission locations. Space station, Mars transit, Moon base and Mars base, each with its measured background radiation, gravity and signal delay, and advice that changes with the distance.

No link to Earth needed. It installs as an app and keeps running offline. Check ins and events are stored on the device and sent when the link comes back, like a delayed downlink. A short report for the flight surgeon is ready for the next communication window.

Training drills let anyone test it: oxygen leak, heart rhythm problem, suit cooling failure, sleep loss, cabin oxygen drop, CO2 scrubber failure and a solar storm, plus a replay of the strongest real flare of the week.

Real NASA data

I loaded the real blood results of the four Inspiration4 crew members from NASA OSDR study OSD-575, seven visits from 92 days before launch to 194 days after landing, and ran the triage rules on them. They caught something I did not expect: three of the four crew show very low blood sugar at the same visit 45 days after landing. A real drop in three people at once is unlikely, so the system treats it as a probable sample handling problem and asks for a fresh sample instead of raising an alarm. Live solar flares and particle events come from NASA DONKI, and the background radiation, dose limits and the five hazards come from NASA measurements and standards.

How it works

The interface is a single web page in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with canvas waveforms, so it loads fast on any laptop or tablet. A service worker makes it work offline. The backend is a set of serverless functions on Vercel in Node.js with a Supabase Postgres database. Row level security is on and all keys stay on the server. Wearable sensors can post readings to the API with a device key, and every reading is triaged on the server too. Space weather comes from the NASA DONKI API at the Community Coordinated Modeling Center and is cached. Speech goes to Google Gemini only for transcription and symptom extraction.

The live vital signs in the demo are simulated, using published values for radiation and bone loss so they behave like a real deep space crew. The Inspiration4 blood results are real. This is a prototype and not a medical device.

Why it matters

On a long mission a small problem caught early stays small. I wanted a tool any crew member can read in seconds under stress, that explains itself, and that knows when the crew can handle something and when to call for help. On Earth the same idea helps anyone far from a doctor, from Antarctic stations to ships and rural clinics.

Tools

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, Web Audio, Web Speech, Service Worker, Node.js, Vercel, Supabase Postgres, Google Gemini API, NASA DONKI API, Barlow font from Google Fonts, GitHub.

Code: https://github.com/jubyuhanna-create/Zero-Hour-Protocol

Use of AI

A large part of the code, the interface text and the first draft of this description were written with Claude by Anthropic. I chose the challenge angle, the features and the design, and reviewed and tested the result. The code files and the README carry a note that AI helped write them. The app itself uses Google Gemini at runtime only to transcribe what an astronaut says and turn it into a list of symptoms. Gemini does not make medical decisions, my own rule based triage does, and it is checked against the sensors. The demo video was edited with AI assistance: Claude wrote the code that built the titles, captions, animations and pop ups around real screen recordings of the app, and the music and sounds were generated by that code. The narration voice was generated with Google AI Studio text to speech from my script. The video carries a visible watermark saying it was edited with AI assistance. No NASA logos, branding or design elements were generated or modified.
